evidence: setupRoutes registers Express handlers (app.post, app.patch, app.get), which is transport work for the infrastructure layer
The POST /api/orders handler only checks the request shape (`!customerId || !items || !Array.isArray(items)`) and then calls deps.placeOrderUseCase.execute
The PATCH /api/orders/:orderId/state handler passes the state to deps.updateOrderStateUseCase.execute and makes no transition decision itself
The GET /api/orders/:orderId handler calls deps.orderRepository.getById and maps a missing order to a 404, which is a plain read with no business rule
Every catch block turns the error message into a 400 JSON response, which is HTTP error handling
parsedVerdict.reasoning: src/infrastructure/routes.ts belongs to the infrastructure layer and only does HTTP transport work. It registers Express routes, reads params, query and body from the request, and checks that the request has the right shape (fields present, `items` is an array). It hands each request to an application use case, turns the result into an HTTP status and JSON response, and turns exceptions into 400 errors. None of the routes contains a domain or business rule: the file makes no state-transition decisions, does no stock checks and does no pricing. One route, GET /api/orders/:orderId, calls deps.orderRepository.getById directly instead of going through a use case. That is a simple read with no business logic, and a 404 for a missing order is transport behaviour, so it does not move a responsibility into the wrong layer. Which layers this file may depend on is checked by other tools and is out of scope here.
